title: Strategic Verification for Long-Running LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from single-turn text generators into long-running systems capable of multi-step reasoning, tool use, persistent memory, and reusable skill development. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve agent reliability, but existing approaches commonly treat verification as a fixed component of the reward structure, creating challenges related to sparse credit assignment, verifier reliability, reward hacking, path compliance, and verification cost. We introduce Budgeted Adaptive Verification with Asymmetric Rewards (BAVAR), a framework that formulates verification as a sequential, resource-constrained decision problem. BAVAR selectively determines what to verify, when verification is valuable, which verifier to invoke, and how verified evidence should influence learning based on uncertainty, action criticality, verifier reliability, expected verification value, and remaining computational budget. It combines reliability-gated positive process rewards with persistent penalties for path violations and extends verification to persistent memories and reusable skills. In an illustrative evaluation under matched verification budgets, BAVAR achieved 72.6% safe verified success, compared with 67.1% for uniform dense verification and 58.4% for outcome-only RLVR. Relative to dense verification, BAVAR reduced verification cost per safe success by 45.5% while using 47.8% fewer verifier tokens. It also reduced verified path violations to 7.2 per 100 trajectories, compared with 20.4 for outcome-only RLVR, and reduced successful verifier exploitation to 4.8%, compared with 15.9% for a single-judge baseline and 18.6% for outcome-only RLVR. For persistent artifacts, BAVAR achieved 88.7% held-out reuse success, compared with 81.3% for dense verification. These simulated findings suggest that adaptive allocation of verification resources can improve safe agent performance while reducing computational and verification overhead, providing a principled foundation for scalable verification of long-running autonomous agents.

title: From Argumentation to Labeled Logic Program for LLM Verification
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate fluent but incorrect or unsupported statements, commonly referred to as hallucinations. We propose a hallucination detection framework based on a Labeled Logic Program (LLP) architecture that integrates multiple reasoning paradigms, including logic programming, argumentation, probabilistic inference, and abductive explanation. By enriching symbolic rules with semantic, epistemic, and contextual labels and applying discourse-aware weighting, the system prioritizes nucleus claims over peripheral statements during verification. Experiments on three benchmark datasets and a challenging clinical narrative dataset show that LLP consistently outperforms classical symbolic validators, achieving the highest detection accuracy when combined with discourse modeling. A human evaluation further demonstrates that logic-assisted explanations improve both hallucination detection accuracy and user trust. The results suggest that labeled symbolic reasoning with discourse awareness provides a robust and interpretable approach to LLM verification in safety-critical domains.

title: Trust but Verify: A Verification-First Workflow for LLM-Assisted Legacy Code Migration
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can translate code between frameworks, languages and platform versions at a speed no human team can match, which makes them attractive for modernizing legacy software. Speed, however, shifts the bottleneck from writing code to trusting it. A migrated module that compiles and looks idiomatic may still change behavior in subtle ways, and legacy systems are precisely the systems least likely to have tests that would reveal such changes. This paper proposes a verification-first workflow in which behavioral evidence is established before any code is generated. The workflow has four gates: (1) capture current behavior with characterization tests; (2) generate the migration in small, reviewable units; (3) verify equivalence by differential testing of old and new implementations on the same inputs; and (4) review residual risk with a structured checklist that targets known LLM failure modes. We define a taxonomy of migration defects, metrics for migration trustworthiness, and an evaluation protocol. The workflow treats the LLM as a fast but fallible collaborator whose output is accepted only on evidence.

title: Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation: Human-Routed External Verification Without Inter-Model Deliberation
abstract: When multiple large language models are consulted on the same question, agreement is often treated as evidence of reliability. That inference is weak when models share training data, development pipelines, or alignment methods, and a divergence-triggered procedure cannot address identical correlated errors. This paper isolates a narrower, tractable object: the procedural interval between visible inter-model divergence and final decision. We develop Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation (OMT), a low-machinery verification procedure. Models are queried separately, without access to one another's outputs and without debate, critique, or synthesis. Their divergences are preserved and classified before cross-exposure. A human observer selects decision-relevant divergences and routes each, by type, to grounding independent of the output chain under review. The verification chain ends with the return of grounding, not a synthesized verdict; final adoption is a separate, recorded human judgment. OMT retains five authorities on the human side: salience, routing, sufficiency, stopping, and final adoption. Each is assigned to a named decision-maker, with dispositions and stated grounds recorded. Cases with no observed divergence, or no selected divergence, close as screening prefixes and do not certify agreement. Because the observer is fallible, the method requires observation-condition logging and, in repeated deployment, an error-model ledger that includes both human and model failure modes. The paper defines the constitutive conditions, verification stages, provenance requirements, risk tiers, and failure modes of OMT. Four author-reported development episodes motivate the framework but do not validate it. OMT does not claim superiority over deliberation protocols or improved decision accuracy. Its designed contribution is narrower: to make the path from divergence to external grounding, and from grounding to adoption, attributable and inspectable.

title: LLM-Aided Verification Gap Detection: A Methodology for Identifying Missing Checkers in UVM Testbenches
abstract: High code coverage does not guarantee complete verification. Coverage metrics measure where tests exercise the design, but not whether outputs are actually checked. This gap between exercising code and validating results-the verification gap-allows bugs to escape even with 99%+ coverage. When outputs differ between correct and faulty RTL, but all tests still pass, checkers are missing. This paper presents a novel methodology for identifying verification gaps through LLM-aided analysis of mutation-induced behavioral divergence. The approach combines automated fault injection with structured LLM prompting to systematically detect missing checkers that coverage metrics cannot reveal. The theoretical foundation rests upon a constructive proof: injection of semantically non-equivalent mutations into golden RTL, followed by differential simulation, exposes precisely those output behaviors that evade checker scrutiny. The workflow is straightforward: (i) introduce a small change (mutation) to the RTL, (ii) run the same tests on both original and mutated versions, (iii) if outputs differ but tests pass, a gap exists, (iv) use an LLM to suggest the missing checker, and (v) validate the fix. The entire detection cycle takes about 80 seconds per mutation. Proof-of-concept validation on two representative IP blocks-a round-robin arbiter (350 LOC, algorithmic complexity) and synchronous FIFO (150 LOC, numeric boundaries)-demonstrates methodology feasibility: 4× time reduction, 100% precision (zero false positives), and cross-domain applicability across distinct fault morphologies. Break-even analysis yields N * ≈ 10 faults for initial deployment with asymptotic reduction to N * ≈ 2 upon amortization. The results establish feasibility of LLM-aided gap detection as a complement to traditional coverage-driven verification.

title: StepCache: Step-Level Reuse with Lightweight Verification and Selective Patching for LLM Serving
abstract: Abstract                                      We address LLM serving workloads where repeated requests share a common solution structure but differ in localized constraints such as output schema, variable names, or numeric constants. Prior caching approaches typically reuse either full responses (semantic caching) or model-internal KV/prefix states, which are brittle under partial changes or tightly coupled to specific backends. We present                    StepCache                    , a backend-agnostic step-level reuse layer that segments outputs into ordered steps, retrieves the best matching cached request, verifies steps using lightweight task-aware checks, and regenerates only failing regions through selective patching. StepCache also supports strict structured-output enforcement for JSON through single-step extraction, required-key constraints, and one-shot repair, and includes conservative skip-reuse fallbacks for semantic changes. For linear equations, StepCache promotes verification into correction via a bounded repair loop with a deterministic fallback that guarantees correctness when the backend model fails. In a CPU-only perturbation-heavy micro-benchmark on math and JSON variants (10 base prompts per task with 3 variants per perturbation, totaling 222 evaluation requests per seed), averaged over three seeds (42–44), StepCache reduces mean latency from 2.13 seconds to 0.67 seconds (median: 2.42 seconds to 0.01 seconds; p95: 3.38 seconds to 3.30 seconds), reduces total token usage from 36.1k to 27.3k (162.7 to 123 tokens per request), and improves end-to-end correctness from 72.5% to 100% under both task-specific checks and a stitched-output integrity check. Across requests, 79.7% take the reuse-only fast path, 5.4% require patching, and 14.9% trigger skip-reuse.

title: LLM-as-Critic: Contrastive and Adversarial Strategies for Authentic Text Verification
abstract: The rapid proliferation of sophisticated large language models (LLMs) has revolutionized content generation but concurrently poses significant challenges for distinguishing human-authored from AI-generated text. Traditional detection methods often struggle with the increasing fluency of LLM outputs and their vulnerability to adversarial manipulations. In response, we propose LLM-as-Critic, a novel discriminative framework that fine-tunes a pre-trained LLM to act as an expert judge of textual authenticity. Our method integrates a multi-objective training paradigm encompassing Binary Cross-Entropy loss for fundamental classification, a bespoke Contrastive Learning loss to maximize inter-class separation, and an Adversarial Training scheme to bolster robustness against sophisticated AI-generated content. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets, including news, creative writing, and academic papers, consistently demonstrate LLM-as-Critic's superior performance, achieving F1 scores up to 0.97, significantly outperforming baselines such as Perplexity-based Detectors, Stylometric Feature Analyzers, and Fine-tuned RoBERTa Classifiers. Furthermore, ablation studies validate the incremental contribution of each training component, while human evaluation confirms a higher agreement rate with our model's classifications, reinforcing its practical utility. LLM-as-Critic establishes a new state-of-the-art in AI-generated text detection, particularly excelling in generalization to unseen generators and resilience against adversarial attacks.

title: A Risk-Oriented Verification and Validation Framework for Hallucination Detection in Public-Sector LLM Systems
abstract: Abstract                   Large language models (LLMs) are now used in procedural guidance and decision-making in legal information services and in public-sector administrative systems, not only to supplement human judgment but also to serve as a replacement for it. These systems, even though they seem fluent, are also likely to engage in hallucination, which is the creation of appropriate and convincing content not backed up by facts. Hallucination within the framework of the public sector is not only a technical flaw but a risk of governance and operation because erroneous procedural guidance or misleading legal foundations can weaken the legal certitude, administrative responsibility, and civic trust. The previous literature on hallucination detection has mainly been model-based or grounded on retrieval methods, unlikely to do well in practical limits of deployment such as black-box LLM APIs and fewer retraining options. This paper suggests a risk-based verification and validation (V&V) model that redefines the problem of hallucination processing as a governance issue and not an accuracy-focused activity. The model proposes a slot-based separation in line with the administrative methodology and it incorporates cross sample instability, coverage of citation and rule based validation into a composite Hallucination Risk Index. Examples of quantitative risk indicators transformed into operational decisions, such as conditional response, or deferral or escalation to human officers, are illustrative examples of situations in the public sector. The suggested framework puts hallucination management in line with the conventional wisdom of system and software assurance by integrating the hallucination evaluation into the ISO/IEC-style verification and validation artefacts, which offers a viable and verifiable course of action towards responsible use of the LLM-based systems in government administration.

title: DAI: A Domain-Specific LLM with Model-Excluded Authority, Capability-Disjoint Verification, and Recomputable Receipts
abstract: We describe DAI (Decripte Artificial Intelligence), a deployed system in which a software agent conducts an incident-response episode end to end — curating a signal, extracting a target from structured evidence, selecting a reviewed playbook, emitting an action contract, having that contract adjudicated by a decision function that is pure in its declared inputs, executing at a network edge, verifying through a credential provably incapable of writing, sealing a hash-linked transcript, and returning on a schedule to review, reconcile, and undo — with no human approving any step.  <div>  <br> </div> <div>  The system’s contributions as an artifact are: (i) a decision function δ(a, λ, h) whose domain excludes every learned output, making independence from the model a consequence of the signature rather than of a runtime check; (ii) separation of duties realized as capability disjointness between two credentials, verified empirically against the enforcement provider’s API before deployment — the verifying credential receives an authentication error when it attempts to write; (iii) a receipt satisfying a recomputation contract, recomputed in production by a verifier importing none of the system’s code, with exact tamper localization demonstrated by controlled alteration; (iv) per-principal perimeters inside a shared enforcement domain, requiring containment predicates that conjoin a hostname discriminator with the source address, and an aggregation scheme that multiplies simultaneous-containment capacity by the expression-length limit under a platform rule budget; (v) an element-identified reconciliation algorithm that remains sound under that aggregation, where the conventional rule-identified algorithm is unsound in both directions; and (vi) a domain language model trained exclusively on the system’s own outcome-verified transcripts, which narrates and is structurally incapable of deciding. </div> <div>  <br> </div> <div>  We report production measurements: a containment executed, verified by a distinct credential, and sealed 887 ms after the episode’s first turn, including two round trips to the enforcement provider; a receipt of twelve turns recomputed externally with all links valid and, under single-character alteration of turn zero, failing at exactly the altered index; zero-blast-radius isolation confirmed by the absence of any domain-wide rule for the contained address; and the full testimony→review→undo cycle closing. We also report ten defects found in the period, every one of which was silent, and analyse what each revealed. </div>

title: LLM-Based Language Verification and Multimodal Ensemble for Spoken Language Recognition
Ratification by Re-execution: A Dual-agent Protocol for Independent Verification in Legally Consequential LLM Pipelines
abstract: <div>  When a pipeline's output carries legal weight, a verifier that reads an implementer's claims and reasons about them produces an opinion. What a compliance record requires is primary execution evidence produced independently of those claims. This paper presents a dual-agent coordination protocol in which the verifying agent re-executes the production pipeline directly, before reading the implementing agent's self-verification results, and posts its findings as first-hand evidence with file-and-line citations to the live codebase. We call this ratification to distinguish it from review, critique, scoring, and debate. Ratification is the act of confirming a claim through independent re-execution of the system the claim describes, not through reasoning about the claim itself.&nbsp; </div> <div>  &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;The protocol is mediated by two directional append-only outbox files on a shared filesystem. Each file has exactly one writer. A filesystem watcher fires on each file when new content is appended, waking the opposing agent without polling. Neither agent can modify what the other has written. Retraction is public, timestamped, and permanent. The outbox files serve simultaneously as coordination channel, audit trail, and session memory across sessions measured in days.&nbsp; </div> <div>  &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; We demonstrate the protocol in a multi-week production session on a candidate screening system operating under EU AI Act Article 9 risk management, Article 13 transparency, and Article 15 accuracy and robustness requirements. In a two-hour sample window spanning 237 coordination cycles, the protocol surfaces twelve distinct defect classes with zero regressions across a monotonically growing test suite reaching 4,851 passing tests. Eight defects originate in the implementing agent's work and are caught by the verifying agent's independent re-execution. Four originate in the verifying agent's own output and are caught by the same mechanism applied symmetrically. The execution asymmetry between the two agents, one orchestrating multi-phase parallel subagent workflows and the other executing the production chain directly without orchestration, is the structural condition that makes genuine independence possible and that distinguishes this protocol from all prior multi-agent verification approaches. To our knowledge, no prior work demonstrates a dual-agent verification protocol sustaining zero regressions across a session of this duration in a legally consequential production pipeline. </div>

title: Confidence Is Not Probability: Verification-Based Confidence Prediction for LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
abstract: Objective. Token-level confidence estimates from large language models (LLMs) do not reflect whether a generated clinical summary is factually correct. We investigate whether verification-based confidence prediction improves upon token-level estimates and whether LLM-as-judge labels can be assumed reliable for clinical summarization evaluation. Methods. Using MIMIC-IV, we construct 500 clinical summarization tasks across four open-source LLMs (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, Phi-4, Llama-3.1-8B), producing 2,000 primary summaries and 1,500 self-consistency samples. Each summary is scored on 26 verification features spanning coverage, factual consistency, natural language inference, numerical accuracy, semantic similarity, and self-consistency. Ground-truth labels are generated by Codex-GPT-5 and validated by two board-certified physicians on 200 summaries. Results. Three judges produce markedly different label distributions (Codex-GPT-5: 93.4% problematic, Phi-4: 10.5%, physicians: 59.5%) with near-zero pairwise agreement ($\kappa = 0.009$–$0.151$). Each physician independently identified only 1 of 200 summaries as fully trustworthy. ClinTrust achieves AUROC = 0.846 [95% CI: 0.788, 0.896] against Codex-GPT-5 labels and 0.695 [0.619, 0.768] against physician labels, significantly outperforming single-feature baselines including token log-probability (0.583) and BERTScore-F1 (0.607). Conclusions. Multi-source verification improves upon token-level confidence for predicting summary reliability, but LLM-as-judge labels are highly variable and cannot be assumed reliable without human validation.
